newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Jospin says Germans resort to EMU fudge.
newsitem.headline: France's Jospin says Germans resort to EMU fudge.

text.p: French Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin accused Germany's conservative government on Wednesday of resorting to accounting devices to qualify for a single European currency.

Jospin, who would probably be prime minister if the left wins next Sunday's crucial parliamentary election runoff, told RTL radio: "Now we learn that the German minister of economics and finance is planning to revalue the country's gold reserves differently to make it easier to meet the Maastricht criteria.
"Our German friends, who are so rigorous about the criteria, are looking to see if they can't fudge things," he said.

Jospin suggested it was time Germany stopped lecturing its European partners on financial rigour and ruling out any talk of flexibility in applying the criteria for European economic and monetary union (EMU).

He cited the German gold move to support his argument that it is wrong to take too narrow an interpretation of the conditions for EMU -- a stance very similar to the centre-right French government's view.

In a move to show that he too has allies in Bonn, Jospin and his German counterpart, Social Democrat (SPD) chairman Oskar Lafontaine, called for the creation of a European "employment pact" to reduce joblessness.

The two said in a joint statement that the single currency could only benefit Europe's citizens if it was accompanied by concrete measures to reduce the current 18 million unemployed across the continent.
Jospin reaffirmed that the Socialists would conduct an audit of French public finances if they win the election, in which the combined left took the lead on the first round last Sunday.
"We want to know where we stand. Not simply on the problem of the public deficit in the strict sense of state finances. What worries us more are the Social Security accounts," he said.

The Central Social Security Agency forecast on April 22 a 35 billion franc deficit this year in the fund which finances public health, welfare and pensions, five billion francs more than the government forecast. But press reports have said the shortfall could higher.

Jospin compared the German gold move with the French government's move to reduce this year's budget deficit by counting as revenue a 37 billion franc payment from state-owned France Telecom to meet future pension liabilities.
"Honestly, things aren't clear today because there are exercises in budgetary disguise," Jospin said. "The France Telecom issue is one such example."

He has said he supports EMU provided the criteria, and particularly the limit on public deficits of three percent of gross domestic product, are interpreted flexibly to allow countries such as Spain and Italy to join from the start.

In their joint statement, Jospin and Lafontaine called on the European Union to include employment targets within "the front line of its decision-making" and for a specific chapter on jobs policy to be included in a revised Maastricht Treaty.

They called for increased training opportunities and a requirement on trade unions and employers that wage and employment policies be focussed on ways to create more jobs through the use of productivity gains.
Corporate taxes should be harmonised across the continent to prevent so-called "tax-dumping", where employers flock to those countries with the most favourable tax regimes, they said.
"Monetary union is no end in itself. The euro will only meet with the approval of Europe's citizens if currency union promotes growth, employment and stability in all member states," they concluded.
